concepts_taught.name: meet-in-the-middle cryptanalysis and what a reduced-round attack means: working forward from the plaintext and backward from the ciphertext to trade one enormous search for two smaller ones plus a lookup, the safety margin between the rounds you can break and the rounds that ship, and how an invariant fingerprint deletes an enumeration step outright

why a stateful protocol can't run serverless: a live session pins requests to the machine holding it, blocking plain load balancing and scale-to-zero — and the stateless-request answer the web reached decades ago, with state pushed out to whatever the client carries
reentrancy and idempotency as the enabling discipline for massively parallel pipelines: if retrying is always safe, recovery is one line and partial state never has to be reasoned about

the parameter count as three separable costs — bytes resident in fast memory (parameters times bits per weight), bytes read per token (the bandwidth bound that sets decode speed), and arithmetic per token — which moved in lockstep only in a plain dense transformer, and the four-number spec sheet (resident bytes at your precision, bytes read per token, active parameters, KV cache at real context) that replaces it

why Kaplan et al. (2020) defined model size N as excluding all vocabulary and positional embeddings (N is about 12 times layers times hidden size squared), and reported that including embedding parameters obscures the scaling trend by making loss appear to depend separately on depth

per-layer embeddings as a mechanism: each decoder layer gets its own token-indexed embedding table; token IDs index the per-layer table while the normal token embedding is projected into the same space, the combined layer-specific slice is gated by the hidden state after the feed-forward residual update, projected back to hidden size, normalized and added as a second residual — costing a lookup rather than a matmul, so the tables can be cached to fast storage outside accelerator memory (Gemma 3n E2B: over 5B loaded under standard execution vs 1.91B effective memory load; Gemma 4 E2B: 2.3B effective / 5.1B total)

why MoE and per-layer embeddings are opposite trades reported in the same unit: MoE cuts arithmetic per token while leaving the memory footprint (Gemma 4 26B A4B activates 4B per token but all 26B must be loaded, 57.7 GB in BF16), PLE cuts the fast-memory footprint while leaving the compute core's arithmetic

why 'effective parameters' is a claim about a deployment rather than a property of a checkpoint — the same Google documentation lists Gemma 4 E2B at both a 1.91B effective memory load and 11.4 GB in BF16, depending on whether the runtime implements PLE offload

why robots.txt disallow and the noindex meta tag are different instructions — blocking the crawl prevents the crawler from ever reading the in-page do-not-index directive, so a linked-to URL gets indexed anyway; and why 'public URL plus unguessable token' is a security model with exactly one failure condition

per-layer embeddings and the model-weights memory hierarchy: why an embedding table is a lookup rather than a computation, so it can live in flash and be read a few hundred bytes at a time per token, while only the compute core needs fast memory — and why 'all weights resident at once' is an inherited convention rather than a requirement

the legal state of AI training data: fair use as a deliberately open-ended four-factor defense (transformative use, and factor-four market/dilution harm), the three 2025 rulings (Ross = not fair use/non-generative, Bartz = training transformative but pirated acquisition infringing, Kadrey = fair use on these facts with the market-dilution door open), and the copyright/contract split — why ProCD-style Section 301 non-preemption lets a terms-of-service clause forbid distillation even where training itself is fair use, making input-freeing and output-freeing proposals pull against each other

why a reasoning-effort dial can be non-monotonic for coding: a model tuned to verify and iterate will, given more budget on a small well-scoped task, spend it on unsolicited refactoring/over-verification, which graders penalize as errors

what 'cleaning' a large code corpus actually means: language detection, per-file license detection, MinHash near-deduplication (why dedup prevents a corpus from becoming a popularity contest), quality filtering, and PII redaction — and why provenance/auditability is the payoff rather than raw model quality

CUDA is a layered stack, not a language: the driver, the PTX virtual instruction set lowered in a second step to per-architecture machine code (SASS/cubin), the nvcc compiler, and fifteen-plus years of hand-tuned libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL, CUTLASS) — and why the tuning and edge-case fixes, not the API surface, are the actual barrier

ROCm as a component-for-component mirror of CUDA (HIP mirrors the CUDA language layer, hipify source-translates, rocBLAS/MIOpen/RCCL/rocFFT mirror cuBLAS/cuDNN/NCCL/cuFFT), and why the hard 20% is missing/slow/numerically-divergent kernels — floating-point non-associativity making 'correctness' a long-tail QA problem rather than a checkbox

the three strategies for crossing the CUDA moat: rebuild the mirror (ROCm), compatibility/translation layers at source or binary level (hipify, ZLUDA, SCALE) which stay one release behind, and routing around CUDA via the framework layer

the framework-abstraction bridge: almost no one hand-writes CUDA (they write PyTorch); Triton (OpenAI, 2021) is an MLIR-based kernel language with a swappable backend that lowers to NVIDIA PTX or AMD GCN, and PyTorch 2.0's torch.compile emits Triton by default — making a chip a backend flag rather than a rewrite, with the Gluon dialect (2025) as the leak where peak performance still needs architecture-specific code

why the moat has moved from single-node kernel software up to disaggregated multi-GPU inference and networking: with AI agents now able to write/optimize kernels, the durable barrier becomes collective communication and interconnect at system scale (NCCL/RCCL parity, network-card software), which compose unreliably on rivals — and why inference falls first and frontier training last

why RL post-training hits a memory wall that inference does not: backpropagation requires retained forward activations, and group-relative policy optimization multiplies that by several responses branching off one shared history

the recompute-instead-of-store trade in the lineage of gradient checkpointing, and LongStraw's sharpening of it — keep the shared prompt as compact model-native resident state, score non-trained branches graph-free, rebuild only the policy response under autograd, then pop back to the prompt boundary

distillation as three conflated things: true distillation (training a student on the teacher's full output distribution, which commercial APIs do not serve), fine-tuning on sampled completions (cheap, common, a ToS violation of unsettled legal status), and mere convergence from overlapping web data — plus why identity confusion and stylistic tics are training-data contamination rather than fingerprints

difficulty-adjusted detection of benchmark gaming: regressing a target cell against structurally similar neighbors and testing the residual, rather than reading the raw score, and why a pattern present across the whole sample (60% of all images facing right) is not evidence about any one cell

why the software stack rather than the silicon has been the barrier to a second frontier-training GPU vendor: CUDA as fifteen-plus years of libraries, kernels and tooling, and what it means for a chip vendor to buy a frontier lab's engineering attention to close that gap
agentic abstention (sequential stop/act/gather decisions, and the overall-vs-timely recall split)
reward hacking as a containment risk: an optimizer routing around a sandbox because the shortest path to a high score left the environment

graph-based retrieval (GraphRAG): the four-stage index — chunking with the 600-vs-2400-token extraction tradeoff, LLM entity/relation extraction with gleanings, entity merging into a weighted graph, and hierarchical Leiden community detection with bottom-up community summaries

map-reduce global search: answering against every community summary in parallel, self-assigned 0-100 helpfulness scores as triage for the context budget, and why the graph makes indexing expensive but queries cheap

the two families under one name: community-summary GraphRAG (for query-focused summarization) versus Personalized PageRank over an extracted graph (HippoRAG, for associative multi-hop), and why a random walk gives multi-hop for free but says nothing about corpus-level themes

the evidence audit: ~3-point multi-hop gains over vector RAG at 40-57x index build time, only ~65% of answer entities present in the constructed graph, and LLM-judge order sensitivity undermining the headline win rates

LazyGraphRAG's deferral principle: noun-phrase co-occurrence graph with no LLM at index time, best-first plus breadth-first search at query time, and a single relevance-test-budget knob as the cost-quality dial
why language skill and factual world knowledge scale differently with model size (~4x vs ~21x across 0.5B-72B), and why that makes a small model the right choice for in-pipeline extraction
write contention as the real bottleneck in multi-agent coding, and the planner/worker role split as both a context-economy and a cost-allocation mechanism

dense-reward / partial-credit grading for long-horizon agent benchmarks: why binary pass-fail destroys information on multi-hour tasks, how decomposing a task into graded subtasks yields a 0-to-1 score, and how the gap between the 0.95 and 1.0 thresholds localizes where runs die
why per-token pricing runs roughly five to one output-over-input: prompts are read in one parallel pass while output is generated sequentially, one token at a time

why training memory scales with context length while inference memory does not — the backward pass must retain the entire forward computation to compute gradients, and in GRPO this is multiplied by the group of sampled responses

delta-rule linear attention: replacing the additive/Hebbian outer-product state update with an error-correcting delta update (retrieve the current value for a key, correct by a learned rate beta times the error), its equivalence to one gradient step of online MSE regression, the Widrow-Hoff and fast-weight-programmer lineage, chunkwise-parallel training via the Householder/WY representation, the gating extension (Gated DeltaNet), and the fixed-size-state limit that forces hybrid architectures

why code corpora teach a model what code looks like but not what it does — the file is a description of a process whose outcome is never in the file — and execution traces as the training signal that connects text to consequence
motivated mislabeling: why an LLM judge that is told how its labels will be used grades strategically, and why the eval harness is a participant rather than a measuring instrument
adverse selection in red-teaming: why cross-model failure rates from iteratively-discovered scenarios are an existence proof, not a leaderboard

weak-to-strong generalization: using a weak supervisor to elicit a strong model's latent capabilities, Performance Gap Recovered (PGR), the auxiliary confidence loss, bootstrapping through intermediate models, and the elicitation-vs-teaching debate as the crux of scalable oversight
iterative latent depth: weight-tied recurrent blocks with inner/outer loops, spectral stability constraints, and adaptive early exit as a test-time compute axis
the coding-agent context tax: why tool schemas and system prompts are re-sent every request, and why prefix caching only pays off when the prefix is byte-identical
centaurs and reverse centaurs (the automation-theory distinction between a human assisted by a machine and a machine assisted by a human)
automation complacency and automation bias, and why vigilance cannot be trained into operators
the jagged technological frontier and why AI's competence boundary is invisible from the inside
automation-induced deskilling, and the withdrawal design (measuring unaided performance) as the experiment that detects it
the calibration failure: why self-reported productivity gains are unreliable evidence about AI tools
fused attention kernels and why GPU occupancy is not the same as speed (FlashAttention)
